questions.question: The presence of Frenkel defects in a crystal .................... its density.
questions.answer:
**(C)** does not change

A Frenkel defect is formed when an ion leaves its lattice site and occupies an interstitial position **within the same crystal** — no ion is lost and none is added. Since the mass and the volume stay the same, the density is unaffected. (Schottky defects, where ions are missing altogether, *do* lower the density.) Frenkel defects occur in crystals where the cation and anion differ greatly in size, e.g. AgCl and ZnS; they raise the ionic conductivity without changing density.

questions.question: Radioactive decay follows the .................... kinetics.
questions.answer:
**(C)** first order

Radioactive decay is a first-order process — the number of nuclei disintegrating per second is proportional to the number present:

$$\frac{dN}{dt}=-\lambda N\ \Rightarrow\ N=N_0e^{-\lambda t}$$

Hence the half-life, $t_{1/2}=0.693/\lambda$, is constant and independent of the amount present, which is the experimental signature of first-order kinetics.

questions.question: A 1% solution of Phenol is a/an
questions.answer:
**(B)** disinfectant

A 1% phenol solution is used as a **disinfectant** — it kills micro-organisms on inanimate objects such as floors, drains and instruments. It is too corrosive and toxic to be applied to living tissue; the dilute (0.2–1%) preparations used on skin are classed as antiseptics. (The printed key marks (b), which is correct — phenol at 1% is the classic disinfectant, while stronger phenol was the original antiseptic of Lister.)

questions.question: Amongst the following, the strongest base is
questions.answer:
**(A)** benzylamine

Benzylamine, $\ce{C6H5CH2NH2}$, is a **primary aliphatic-type** amine: the —NH$_2$ is separated from the ring by a CH$_2$ group, so the lone pair is not delocalised and the amine is as basic as ammonia or slightly more ($\text{p}K_b\approx4.7$). Aniline's lone pair is delocalised into the ring ($\text{p}K_b\approx9.4$), and the —NO$_2$ group in p-nitroaniline withdraws electron density further, making it the weakest. Acetanilide is an amide, essentially neutral.

questions.question: A new carbon-carbon bond formation is possible in
questions.answer:
**(B)** Friedel-Crafts reaction

In Friedel-Crafts acylation the acyl carbon, which was part of a separate molecule (an acid chloride), becomes bonded to a ring carbon:

$$\ce{C6H6 + CH3COCl ->[AlCl3] C6H5COCH3 + HCl}$$

So a new C–C bond is created. Cannizzaro (disproportionation of an aldehyde) and Clemmensen (reduction of a ketone) both preserve the number of C–C bonds, and the Reimer-Tiemann reaction forms a C–C bond too, but the standard text-book answer here is Friedel-Crafts as it is the general C–C bond-forming reaction of arenes. *(Reimer-Tiemann, giving salicylaldehyde from phenol, is also formally correct; the printed key marks (b).)*

questions.question: The compound which reacts with HBr in accordance with the Markovnikov's rule is
questions.answer:
**(D)** (CH$_3$)$_2$C=CH$_2$

Markovnikov's rule is only tested when the two carbons of the double bond carry different numbers of hydrogens. In 2-methylpropene the proton adds to the terminal CH$_2$ so that the more stable tertiary carbocation is formed, and bromide then attacks it:

$$\ce{(CH3)2C=CH2 + HBr -> (CH3)2C(Br)CH3}$$

cis- and trans-but-2-ene are symmetrical, so both directions give 2-bromobutane and no preference needs stating; ethyne gives vinyl bromide.

questions.question: Galena is an ore of
questions.answer:
**(D)** Pb

**Galena** is lead(II) sulphide, **PbS**, the principal ore of lead (about 86% Pb). It is concentrated by froth floatation and then roasted to the oxide before reduction:

$$\ce{2PbS + 3O2 -> 2PbO + 2SO2}$$

It is also the chief source of silver, which occurs with it. (Others: haematite Fe$_2$O$_3$; copper pyrite CuFeS$_2$; zinc blende ZnS.)

questions.question: Vitamin C is the compound called
questions.answer:
**(C)** Ascorbic acid

Vitamin C is **ascorbic acid**, a water-soluble vitamin found in citrus fruit and green vegetables. It is a lactone with an enediol group, which is easily oxidised to dehydroascorbic acid — hence its role as an antioxidant and in collagen synthesis; its deficiency causes scurvy. (Riboflavin is vitamin B$_2$; thiamine is vitamin B$_1$; raffinose is a sugar, not a vitamin.)

questions.question: What is glycosidic linkage?
questions.answer:
A **glycosidic linkage** is the **ether bond ($\ce{-O-}$) between the anomeric carbon of one monosaccharide and a hydroxyl group of another** — it is what joins two monosaccharides into a disaccharide, with the loss of a molecule of water:

$$\ce{C6H12O6 + C6H12O6 -> C12H22O11 + H2O}$$

For example, in sucrose an $\alpha$-glucose is joined to a $\beta$-fructose through C-1 of glucose and C-2 of fructose; in maltose the link is $\alpha$-1,4 and in cellobiose $\beta$-1,4. The position and $\alpha$/$\beta$ configuration of the linkage decide whether the polysaccharide is starch, glycogen or cellulose.

questions.question: Write the IUPAC name of K$_3$[Al(C$_2$O$_4$)$_3$].
questions.answer:
**Potassium trioxalatoaluminate(III)**

The complex anion $[\ce{Al(C2O4)3}]^{3-}$ contains three bidentate oxalate (oxalato) ligands and aluminium in the +3 state (if Al is $x$ and each oxalate −2: $x+3(-2)=-3\Rightarrow x=+3$). Three K$^+$ ions balance the charge. The anion is named first, with the ligands in alphabetical order and their number given by the prefix *tri*, and the metal followed by its oxidation state in Roman numerals.

questions.question: Name the monomers of Buna-S rubber.
questions.answer:
**Buna-S** (styrene–butadiene rubber, SBR) is a copolymer of **1,3-butadiene** and **styrene** (phenylethene):

$$\ce{nCH2=CH-CH=CH2 + nC6H5CH=CH2 ->[-Na] [-CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH(C6H5)-CH2-]_n}$$

It is a synthetic rubber, tougher and more abrasion-resistant than natural rubber, used in tyres. ('Bu' comes from butadiene, 'na' from sodium (Na) which is the initiator, and 'S' from styrene.)

questions.question: Give an example of food preservative.
questions.answer:
**Sodium benzoate, $\ce{C6H5COONa}$** — used in soft drinks, jams and sauces at concentrations around 0.1%. Other examples are **sodium metabisulphite ($\ce{Na2S2O5}$)**, **potassium sorbate**, and common salt, sugar and vinegar (acetic acid).

Preservatives work either by lowering the pH so that micro-organisms cannot grow, or by being taken up by the microbial cell and interfering with its metabolism; sodium benzoate is active as the undissociated acid, which is why it works best in acid foods.

questions.question: What are antihistamines?
questions.answer:
**Antihistamines** are drugs that oppose the action of **histamine**, a substance released by mast cells during an allergic reaction that causes vasodilation, itching, sneezing and bronchoconstriction.

The drugs (e.g. **chlorpheniramine, diphenhydramine, promethazine, cetirizine**) are H$_1$-receptor antagonists: they block the histamine receptor sites so that histamine cannot bind, and are used for hay fever, urticaria and motion sickness. Most older ones also cause drowsiness. They are not effective in asthma, because there histamine acts on a different receptor.

questions.question: Give an example of heterogeneous catalysis.
questions.answer:
**The synthesis of ammonia from $\ce{N2}$ and $\ce{H2}$ over iron (Haber's process):**

$$\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) ->[Fe(s)][700 K,\ 200 atm] 2NH3(g)}$$

The catalyst is in one phase (solid iron, promoted with K$_2$O and Al$_2$O$_3$) and the reactants are in another (gases), so the catalysis is heterogeneous. Other examples: oxidation of SO$_2$ to SO$_3$ over $\ce{V2O5}$ (contact process), and hydrogenation of vegetable oil over nickel.

questions.question: Write the IUPAC name of $\ce{CH3-CH(OCH3)-CO-CH(CH3)-Cl}$.
questions.answer:
**2-chloro-4-methoxypentan-3-one**

The chain is numbered to give the ketone the lowest locant (C-3), so the methoxy carbon becomes C-4 and the chlorine-bearing carbon C-2. Alphabetically chloro comes before methoxy:

| C-2 | C-3 | C-4 |
|---|---|---|
| $\ce{Cl, CH3}$ | $\ce{=O}$ | $\ce{OCH3}$ |

So $\ce{CH3-CH(OCH3)-CO-CH(Cl)-CH3}$ is 2-chloro-4-methoxypentan-3-one — the same name the printed key gives.

questions.question: Write the geometrical isomers of [CoCl$_2$(NH$_3$)$_4$]$^+$.
questions.answer:
The complex is octahedral with a coordination number of 6, two Cl$^-$ and four NH$_3$ — an $\ce{MA4B2}$ type, which shows **two geometrical isomers**:

**(i) cis-isomer** — the two Cl ligands occupy adjacent positions (e.g. cis to each other, with one NH$_3$ trans to each Cl).

**(ii) trans-isomer** — the two Cl ligands occupy opposite ends of an axis, all four NH$_3$ then lying in the equatorial plane.

The violet cis form and the green trans form differ in colour and dipole moment (the trans isomer is non-polar, the cis has a net dipole). Since the ligand set is $\ce{M A4 B2}$ there are no optical isomers — the two are the complete set. The printed key draws neither clearly, so both are given above.

questions.question: Write any two functions of RNA found in the cells.
questions.answer:
**(i) It carries and translates the genetic message.** mRNA copies the base sequence of a gene and carries it to the ribosome, where tRNA reads the codon and brings the matching amino acid — so RNA is the working copy of DNA in protein synthesis.

**(ii) It is a structural and catalytic part of the ribosome.** rRNA forms the bulk of the ribosome and provides its shape and catalytic (peptidyl transferase) activity, acting as a ribozyme.

*Other acceptable answers:* some RNAs act as regulatory molecules, and RNA is the genetic material of some viruses.

questions.question: Why do transition metals form complex compounds?
questions.answer:
Because the transition-metal ion has a combination of features that favour coordination:

1. **Small size and high nuclear charge**, hence a high charge density, which strongly attracts ligands.
2. **Vacant d orbitals** of suitable energy — the metal can accept electron pairs from ligands (it acts as a Lewis acid), and hybridisation of $(n-1)d$, $ns$ and $np$ orbitals gives defined geometries.
3. **Variable oxidation states**, so the ion can adjust its charge to suit the ligand.
4. **Ability to form chelates** with polydentate ligands, which is entropically favoured.

The result is a coordinate (dative) bond from ligand to metal, and the complex is stabilised by the resulting crystal-field (ligand-field) stabilisation energy.

questions.question: Write chemical equations for the synthesis of (a) Teflon (b) Neoprene.
questions.answer:
**(a) Teflon** — addition polymerisation of tetrafluoroethylene (made from chloroform and HF):

$$\ce{nCF2=CF2 ->[\text{peroxide}] [-CF2-CF2-]_n}$$

Teflon (polytetrafluoroethylene) is chemically inert and heat-resistant, used for non-stick coatings and laboratory ware.

**(b) Neoprene** — addition polymerisation of chloroprene (2-chlorobuta-1,3-diene):

$$\ce{nCH2=C(Cl)-CH=CH2 ->[\text{peroxide}] [-CH2-C(Cl)=CH-CH2-]_n}$$

Neoprene is a synthetic rubber resistant to oil, heat and weathering, used for hoses, gaskets and wetsuits.

questions.question: Why is limestone added to the blast furnace in the extraction of iron from haematite?
questions.answer:
**Limestone ($\ce{CaCO3}$) is added as a flux to remove the silica impurity as slag.**

In the hot furnace the limestone decomposes:

$$\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$$

The quicklime so formed combines with the silica (sand) of the ore to give molten calcium silicate:

$$\ce{CaO + SiO2 -> CaSiO3}\quad(\text{slag})$$

Calcium silicate is liquid at the furnace temperature and, being much less dense than iron, **floats on the molten iron** and is run off separately — so it removes the acidic gangue that would otherwise contaminate the metal. The iron itself is reduced by carbon monoxide from burning coke, since iron lies below carbon in the reactivity series:

$$\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$$

(Note the printed answer muddles this: it says limestone removes silica — correct — but then speaks of silicon being present as an impurity and of iron being reduced 'by heating with carbon', whereas in the upper part of the furnace the reducing agent is CO.)

questions.question: Define molar conductivity of a substance. How does it vary with concentration for weak and strong electrolytes?
questions.answer:
**Molar conductivity, $\Lambda_m$,** is the conductivity of a solution containing one mole of electrolyte placed between two electrodes 1 cm apart (i.e. of unit volume):

$$\Lambda_m=\frac{\kappa}{c}\qquad(\text{S cm}^2\ \text{mol}^{-1}\ \text{if } c \text{ is in mol cm}^{-3})$$

It expresses how efficiently a given amount of electrolyte conducts, correcting for how much of it is present.

**Variation with concentration.**

- **Strong electrolytes** (KCl, NaCl, HCl): $\Lambda_m$ decreases only slightly, roughly linearly with $\sqrt{c}$, because the number of ions per unit volume is high and inter-ionic attractions slow them. Extrapolating to $c\to0$ gives the limiting value $\Lambda_m^\circ$ — this is what Kohlrausch's law of independent migration is based on.
- **Weak electrolytes** (CH$_3$COOH, NH$_4$OH): $\Lambda_m$ rises very steeply at low concentration because the degree of dissociation increases sharply on dilution, and it cannot be obtained by extrapolation; $\Lambda_m^\circ$ is found by Kohlrausch's law instead.

In both cases conductivity $\kappa$ itself *increases* with concentration while $\Lambda_m=\kappa/c$ falls.

questions.question: 6.02×10$^{22}$ molecules of urea are present in 100 ml of its solution. What is the concentration of the urea solution?
questions.answer:
Number of moles of urea:

$$n=\frac{6.02\times10^{22}}{6.02\times10^{23}}=10^{-1}=0.1\ \text{mol}$$

Volume of solution $=100\ \text{mL}=0.1\ \text{L}$, so

$$M=\frac{n}{V}=\frac{0.1}{0.1}=1\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

**The solution is 1 M.**

*(The printed key slips a factor of ten: it divides $6.02\times10^{22}$ by $6.02\times10^{23}$ and writes $10^{-3}$ where the quotient is $10^{-1}$, then gets 0.01 M. With $6.02\times10^{22}$ molecules in 100 mL the correct molarity is 1 M — the arithmetic $n=0.1$, $V=0.1$ L is unambiguous.)*

questions.question: Distinguish between molarity and molality.
questions.answer:
| Molarity (M) | Molality (m) |
|---|---|
| Number of moles of solute per **litre of solution** | Number of moles of solute per **kilogram of solvent** |
| Depends on temperature, since the volume of a liquid changes with temperature | Independent of temperature, since masses do not change |
| Units: mol L$^{-1}$ | Units: mol kg$^{-1}$ |
| Convenient for preparing a solution of known volume in the laboratory | Preferred for accurate work and for colligative properties |
| Affected by the volume of the solute as well as of the solvent | Depends only on the mass of solvent |

Molarity is the practical, volumetric measure; molality is the thermodynamic one used in freezing-point and boiling-point work. *(The printed table has the two columns' definitions swapped in the first row — corrected above.)*

questions.question: Complete the following: (i) $\ce{P4 + HNO3 ->}$ (ii) $\ce{Ca3P2 + H2O ->}$ (iii) $\ce{NaClO4 + HCl ->}$
questions.answer:
**(i)** Hot concentrated nitric acid oxidises white phosphorus to phosphoric acid, itself being reduced to NO$_2$ (brown fumes):

$$\ce{P4 + 20HNO3 -> 4H3PO4 + 20NO2 + 4H2O}$$

**(ii)** Calcium phosphide is hydrolysed to phosphine:

$$\ce{Ca3P2 + 6H2O -> 3Ca(OH)2 + 2PH3 ^}$$

Phosphine, $\ce{PH3}$, is a colourless, highly poisonous gas with a fishy smell, and is spontaneously flammable.

**(iii)** Sodium perchlorate with concentrated hydrochloric acid gives perchloric acid and sodium chloride — a strong, non-oxidising acid displacing a weaker one from its salt:

$$\ce{NaClO4 + HCl -> HClO4 + NaCl}$$

Concentrated perchloric acid is a strong oxidising agent when hot and is dangerous with organic matter.

questions.question: Describe with the help of chemical equations the preparation of potassium dichromate from chromite ore.
questions.answer:
Chromite ore, $\ce{FeCr2O4}$ (chromium in the +3 state), is oxidised to chromate(VI) and then converted to the dichromate.

**Step 1 — fusion with alkali in air.** Powdered chromite is fused with sodium carbonate (or NaOH) in the presence of air:

$$\ce{4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 -> 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2 ^}$$

(or, with NaOH, $\ce{4FeCr2O4 + 16NaOH + 7O2 -> 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8H2O}$). The chromium is oxidised from +3 to +6; the yellow solution of sodium chromate is filtered from the iron(III) oxide.

**Step 2 — acidification to dichromate.**

$$\ce{2Na2CrO4 + H2SO4 -> Na2Cr2O7 + Na2SO4 + H2O}$$

A dichromate is stable only in acidic solution; the yellow chromate turns orange.

**Step 3 — conversion to the potassium salt.** Potassium chloride is added, and the less soluble potassium dichromate crystallises out:

$$\ce{Na2Cr2O7 + 2KCl -> K2Cr2O7 + 2NaCl}$$

Potassium dichromate is less soluble than the sodium salt and so separates as the orange-red crystals, which are filtered off and recrystallised.

questions.question: Explain the following reactions with an example in each case: (i) Sandmeyer's reaction (ii) Diazotisation reaction.
questions.answer:
**(i) Sandmeyer's reaction.** Treatment of a freshly prepared benzene diazonium salt with a copper(I) halide in the corresponding halogen acid replaces the $\ce{-N2^+}$ group by a halogen, giving an aryl halide:

$$\ce{C6H5N2^+Cl^- + CuCl/HCl -> C6H5Cl + N2 ^ + CuCl2}$$

Analogously the bromide and cyanide give bromobenzene and benzonitrile ($\ce{CuCN/KCN}$). The reaction is used to convert a primary aromatic amine into an aryl halide, which is otherwise hard to obtain.

**(ii) Diazotisation.** A primary aromatic amine is treated with nitrous acid (generated *in situ* from sodium nitrite and a strong acid such as HCl, H$_2$SO$_4$ or HBF$_4$) at 273–278 K:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + NaNO2 + 2HCl ->[273-278 K] C6H5N2^+Cl^- + NaCl + 2H2O}$$

The product, benzene diazonium chloride, is a stable salt only in the cold; it is non-nucleophilic (the diazonium ion is resonance-stabilised) and it is the gateway to a large family of aryl derivatives. Above 278 K it decomposes to phenol and nitrogen.

questions.question: Give reasons for the following: (a) Phenol is more acidic than ethanol. (b) o- and p-nitrophenols are more acidic than phenol.
questions.answer:
**(a) Phenol vs ethanol.** Both are weak acids, but phenol is far the stronger ($\text{p}K_a$ ≈ 10 against ≈ 16). The reason is the **stability of the conjugate base**. In ethanol the alkoxide ion is destabilised by the electron-releasing alkyl group, with the negative charge localised on the oxygen. In phenoxide the charge is **delocalised into the ring** by resonance — it can be written on the ortho and para carbons as well as on oxygen — and the ring offers a larger volume over which to spread it. The more the negative charge is dispersed, the more stable the ion, and the more readily the proton is released.

**(b) Nitrophenols.** The —NO$_2$ group is **strongly electron-withdrawing** (by both $-I$ and $-M$ effects). In the o- and p- positions it can be relayed by resonance into the ring, pulling electron density away from the O–H bond and weakening it, so the proton is lost more easily. The nitrophenoxide ion is then further stabilised, because the negative charge is delocalised onto the nitro group's oxygens as well as the ring. Hence $\text{p}K_a$ falls (o- ≈ 7.2, p- ≈ 7.1, against 10 for phenol). The meta isomer gets only the inductive effect and is barely more acidic than phenol.

questions.question: Define the following terms: (i) Micelles (ii) Peptization (iii) Electrophoresis.
questions.answer:
**(i) Micelles.** Aggregates of surfactant (e.g. soap) molecules in water in which the hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails point inwards and the hydrophilic heads outwards, forming a roughly spherical cluster of colloidal size ($\sim10^{-9}$–$10^{-6}$ m). Above the critical micelle concentration the excess soap forms micelles, which solubilise grease and dirt and allow them to be washed away.

**(ii) Peptization.** The process of converting a **precipitate into a colloidal solution** by adding a small amount of a suitable electrolyte (the peptizing agent), which is adsorbed on the particles and gives them like charges so that they repel and stay dispersed. E.g. ferric hydroxide precipitate is peptised by a little $\ce{FeCl3}$.

**(iii) Electrophoresis.** The **movement of charged colloidal particles in an electric field** towards the oppositely charged electrode. It shows that colloidal particles are electrically charged, and is used to determine the sign of the charge and to separate or deposit proteins and other colloids (e.g. in electrophoresis gels).

questions.question: How will you bring out following conversions? (i) Chlorobenzene to p-nitrophenol (ii) 2-bromopropane to 1-bromopropane (iii) Aniline to phenyl isocyanide
questions.answer:
**(i) Chlorobenzene → p-nitrophenol:** nitration first (the Cl is o/p-directing), then nucleophilic substitution of the activated chloride by hydroxide under pressure, with acidification:

$$\ce{C6H5Cl ->[HNO3][H2SO4] p-ClC6H4NO2 ->[NaOH(aq)][623 K,\ 300 atm] p-NO2C6H4ONa ->[H^+] p-NO2C6H4OH}$$

**(ii) 2-bromopropane → 1-bromopropane:** dehydrohalogenation, then anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr with peroxide:

$$\ce{CH3CH(Br)CH3 ->[KOH(alc)][\Delta] CH3CH=CH2 ->[HBr,\ H2O2] CH3CH2CH2Br}$$

The peroxide effect (free-radical addition) puts the Br on the terminal carbon — the reverse of Markovnikov addition.

**(iii) Aniline → phenyl isocyanide:** the carbylamine reaction, heating with chloroform and alcoholic KOH:

$$\ce{C6H5NH2 + CHCl3 + 3KOH -> C6H5NC + 3KCl + 3H2O}$$

Phenyl isocyanide has an unbearable smell and is the test for a primary amine.

questions.question: Aluminium crystallises in a cubic close packed structure. Its metallic radius is 125 pm. (a) What is the length of the side of the unit cell? (b) How many unit cells are there in 1.00 cm$^3$ of aluminium?
questions.answer:
**(a) Edge of the unit cell.** In a c.c.p. (f.c.c.) structure the atoms touch along the face diagonal, so

$$4r=\sqrt{2}\,a\ \Rightarrow\ a=2\sqrt{2}\,r$$

With $r=125$ pm:

$$a=2\times1.414\times125=354\ \text{pm}\approx3.54\times10^{-8}\ \text{cm}$$

**(b) Number of unit cells in 1 cm$^3$.** Volume of one cell:

$$V=a^3=(3.54\times10^{-8})^3=4.44\times10^{-23}\ \text{cm}^3$$

$$N=\frac{1.00}{4.44\times10^{-23}}=2.25\times10^{22}\ \text{unit cells}$$

**About $2.25\times10^{22}$ unit cells** ($\approx4.5\times10^{22}$ atoms, four per cell). (The printed key writes $2.27\times10^{22}$, from rounding $a$ to 354 pm; both are within rounding.)

questions.question: What will happen to the value of emf of the cell Zn | Zn$^{2+}$ (0.1M) || Cu$^{2+}$ (0.1M) | Cu, if the concentration of the electrolyte in the anode compartment is increased?
questions.answer:
The cell is

$$\ce{Zn + Cu^{2+} -> Zn^{2+} + Cu}$$

with $n=2$, and its emf is given by the Nernst equation:

$$E=E^\circ-\frac{0.0591}{2}\log\frac{[\ce{Zn^{2+}}]}{[\ce{Cu^{2+}}]}$$

At first both concentrations are 0.1 M, so the logarithm is zero and $E=E^\circ=1.10$ V.

If $[\ce{Zn^{2+}}]$ in the anode compartment is **increased**, its value in the numerator of the logarithm rises, so the term subtracted becomes larger and more positive, and **$E$ falls**. Physically, the build-up of Zn$^{2+}$ near the anode opposes the forward dissolution of zinc (Le Chatelier), so the driving force of the cell is reduced and the emf decreases. Increasing the cathode concentration would have the opposite effect.

questions.question: Give reasons for the following: (i) SiF$_6^{2-}$ is known but SiCl$_6^{2-}$ is not. (ii) H$_3$PO$_2$ acts as a monobasic acid. (iii) PbO$_2$ is a stronger oxidising agent than SnO$_2$. (iv) Sulphur exhibits paramagnetic behaviour in vapour state. (v) Bond dissociation energy of F$_2$ is less than that of Cl$_2$.
questions.answer:
**(i) $\ce{SiF6^{2-}}$ known, $\ce{SiCl6^{2-}}$ not.** Silicon is small, so it can accommodate only small ligands around it without steric crowding. Fluorine atoms are small enough for six of them to fit around Si — hence $\ce{SiF6^{2-}}$ forms readily (a consequence of the high lattice/formation energy of the Si–F bond too). Chlorine atoms are much larger and six of them cannot be packed around the small Si atom; the crowding also makes the Si–Cl bonds weak, so $\ce{SiCl6^{2-}}$ is not stable.

**(ii) $\ce{H3PO2}$ is monobasic.** Basicity is decided by the number of **P–OH** groups, since only a hydrogen attached to oxygen is acidic. Hypophosphorous acid has the structure

$$\ce{H2P(O)(OH)}$$

i.e. only **one** P–OH bond; the other two H atoms are directly bonded to phosphorus and are not ionisable. So only one proton is released: it is monobasic ($\ce{H3PO2 <=> H^+ + H2PO2^-}$). For the same reason $\ce{H3PO3}$ is dibasic and $\ce{H3PO4}$ tribasic.

**(iii) PbO$_2$ a stronger oxidising agent than SnO$_2$.** In both oxides the metal is in the +4 state, but for the heavier elements of the group the **+2 state becomes more stable than +4** because of the inert-pair effect (the $6s^2$ pair is poorly shielded and stays bound). Lead therefore readily gains two electrons to become Pb$^{2+}$, so PbO$_2$ is easily reduced and is a powerful oxidising agent (it liberates chlorine from HCl). Tin holds its +4 state firmly, so SnO$_2$ resists reduction.

**(iv) Sulphur paramagnetic in vapour.** At high temperature sulphur vapour contains $\ce{S2}$ molecules that are isoelectronic with $\ce{O2}$. Like $\ce{O2}$, $\ce{S2}$ has **two unpaired electrons in antibonding $\pi^*$ orbitals** (molecular-orbital configuration ending $\pi^{*2}$ apart), which gives it a net magnetic moment. Hence the vapour, though not the solid, is paramagnetic.

**(v) $E(\text{F}_2)<E(\text{Cl}_2)$.** The F–F bond is exceptionally weak because the fluorine atom is very small: the three lone pairs on each atom are forced close together and their **interelectronic repulsion** is large, as is the repulsion between the bonding electron pairs. The bond therefore breaks easily (bond energy ≈ 158 kJ mol$^{-1}$ against 243 for Cl$_2$), which is also why F$_2$ is such a reactive element despite fluorine's small size.

questions.question: Draw the structures of the following compounds: (i) IF$_7$ (ii) H$_2$S$_2$O$_7$ (iii) XeOF$_4$ (iv) S$_8$ (v) H$_3$PO$_3$.
questions.answer:
**(i) $\ce{IF7}$** — iodine(VII) is $sp^3d^3$ hybridised and the molecule is **pentagonal bipyramidal**: five F in a plane at 72° and one F above, one below; all I–F equal, non-polar.

**(ii) $\ce{H2S2O7}$** (pyrosulphuric acid, oleum) — two SO$_4$ tetrahedra sharing one oxygen: $\ce{HO-SO2-O-SO2-OH}$, i.e. each S carries two $\ce{=O}$ and one bridging $\ce{-O-}$, with an —OH at each end.

**(iii) $\ce{XeOF4}$** — xenon(VI) is $sp^3d^2$; a **square pyramidal** molecule with four F in the base plane, one O at the apex by a double bond, and the lone pair occupying the sixth octahedral site.

**(iv) $\ce{S8}$** — a **crown-shaped (puckered) eight-membered ring** with S–S–S angles of about 105°, giving the ring a chair-like zig-zag; this is the structure of rhombic and monoclinic sulphur.

**(v) $\ce{H3PO3}$** (phosphorous acid) — phosphorus(III) is tetrahedral: $\ce{O=P(H)(OH)2}$, i.e. one $\ce{P=O}$, two $\ce{P-OH}$ and **one P–H** bond. The P–H hydrogen is not acidic, which is why the acid is dibasic.

questions.question: Complete the following: (i) benzene + CH$_3$COCl $\xrightarrow{AlCl_3}$ (ii) benzene $\xrightarrow{\text{conc. }H_2SO_4}$ then $\xrightarrow{HNO_3,\,H_2SO_4}$ (iii) $\ce{CH3COONa ->[NaOH][CaO,\Delta]}$ (iv) ethylbenzene $\xrightarrow{KMnO_4,\,KOH,\text{heat}}$ (v) $\ce{CH3COCH3 + I2 + NaOH ->}$
questions.answer:
**(i) Friedel-Crafts acylation** — acetophenone:

$$\ce{C6H6 + CH3COCl ->[AlCl3] C6H5COCH3 + HCl}$$

**(ii) Sulphonation, then nitration** — the —SO$_3$H group is meta-directing, so nitration goes to the meta position: benzenesulphonic acid, then **m-nitrobenzenesulphonic acid**:

$$\ce{C6H6 ->[conc. H2SO4] C6H5SO3H ->[HNO3/H2SO4] m-NO2C6H4SO3H}$$

**(iii) Decarboxylation with soda lime** — methane:

$$\ce{CH3COONa + NaOH ->[CaO][\Delta] CH4 ^ + Na2CO3}$$

**(iv) Side-chain oxidation** — the alkyl chain is oxidised to a carboxyl group, giving potassium benzoate:

$$\ce{C6H5CH2CH3 ->[KMnO4][KOH,\ \Delta] C6H5COOK}$$

(acidification would give benzoic acid).

**(v) Haloform reaction of acetone** — iodoform and sodium acetate:

$$\ce{CH3COCH3 + 3I2 + 4NaOH -> CHI3 v + CH3COONa + 3NaI + 3H2O}$$

*Two tests:* **methyl acetate and ethyl acetate** — the iodoform test: ethyl acetate has a $\ce{CH3CH(OH)-}$ unit and gives yellow iodoform with I$_2$/NaOH, methyl acetate does not. Alternatively hydrolyse each: methyl acetate gives only methanoic acid, ethyl acetate gives ethanoic acid (detected by its smell or by FeCl$_3$ after neutralisation). **Benzaldehyde and benzoic acid** — Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with benzaldehyde only; and benzoic acid effervesces with NaHCO$_3$ while benzaldehyde does not.

questions.question: (a) State the Arrhenius equation for the rate constant of a reaction. (b) Show that for a first order reaction, the time required for half the change is independent of initial concentration. / The half-life of a first order reaction A is 2 mins. How long will it take A to reach (a) 25% of its initial concentration? (b) 10% of its initial concentration?
questions.answer:
**(a) Arrhenius equation.** The rate constant depends on temperature as

$$k=Ae^{-E_a/RT}$$

where $A$ is the frequency (pre-exponential) factor, $E_a$ the activation energy, $R$ the gas constant and $T$ the absolute temperature. In logarithmic form

$$\log k=\log A-\frac{E_a}{2.303RT}$$

so a plot of $\log k$ against $1/T$ is a straight line of slope $-E_a/2.303R$. It shows that $k$ rises steeply with temperature because the fraction of molecules with energy $\ge E_a$ grows exponentially.

**(b) Half-life of a first-order reaction.** For $\ce{A -> products}$, $\text{rate}=k[A]$:

$$\ln\frac{[A]_0}{[A]}=kt$$

At the half-life $[A]=[A]_0/2$:

$$kt_{1/2}=\ln2=0.693\ \Rightarrow\ t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}$$

$t_{1/2}$ depends only on $k$ — **the initial concentration cancels out**, so it is independent of $[A]_0$. This is the defining test of first-order kinetics.

**Numerical, $t_{1/2}=2$ min.** For 25% *remaining*, two half-lives have elapsed:

$$t=2\times2=4\ \text{min}$$

For 10% remaining, $[A]/[A]_0=0.1$, and $k=0.693/2=0.3465\ \text{min}^{-1}$:

$$t=\frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{100}{10}=\frac{2.303}{0.3465}\times1=6.64\ \text{min}$$

**So 4 minutes for 25% and about 6.6 minutes for 10%.**
